newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Grave robbers stalk hungry Russian city.
newsitem.headline: Grave robbers stalk hungry Russian city.

text.p: Even the dead are not safe from Russia's deep economic crisis. Grave robbers, driven by hunger and desperate poverty, are on the rampage in the textile city of Ivanovo, northeast of Moscow.

Unlike the body-snatchers of byegone days when pioneering medical researchers sought human remains for dissection, they come at night in search of more readily saleable graveyard booty, from plastic flowers and metal plaques to tombstones.

The scourge has reached a new intensity in Ivanovo recently as relatives stream to local cemeteries on annual spring pilgrimages to clean up family plots and place new flowers for Sunday's Russian Orthodox Easter and next week's May Day holidays.
"Things have got really bad this spring with the Easter and May holidays coming," Margarita Noskova, the head of services at Ivanovo's Balino cemetery, told Reuters at the weekend.

"There have always been a few idiots and drunks who take things. But now they're stealing anything and everything, wreathes, aluminium plaques, even whole tombstones. It's a disgrace but that's the kind of country we're living in now."

Noskova blamed the "bomzhi", the homeless drunks that have become a feature of Russian cities since the collapse of Soviet communism, for most of the theft. Relatives were complaining in growing numbers of missing ornaments, as well as metal railings and stools and benches families use for graveside contemplation.

But, she said, other, more professional, operators are involved in the traffic that sees the metal sold off to scrap dealers, the granite recycled by masons into new headstones and artificial flowers put back on sale in Ivanovo's street markets.

With the holidays coming, more than a dozen elderly women were selling brightly coloured flowers made of waxed paper at the city's main market. They insisted they made them themselves to supplement pensions which are meagre if they are paid at all.

As the last of the winter snows disappear, the graveyard has become a bright and busy place, with relatives painting the railings and gates that surround most of the family plots and stringing flowers around the tombstones in an annual ritual.
But here and there the robbers' marks are evident, where aluminum plaques engraved with names have been ripped off.
The local newspaper, Rabochy Krai, said ominously that "fertile soil" from city graveyards was on sale around town.

Burke and Hare, the notorious Edinburgh bodysnatchers who added a new twist at the turn of the 19th century by taking up murder to save time, got their just desserts at the hands of the law. No such fate may await the Ivanovo grave robbers.

The police refuse to take the problem seriously, Noskovo said, even though a plastic wreath can cost the equivalent of up to $30 -- a month's income for many of the town's cotton mill workers -- and a fancy stone might be worth more than $1,000.

The municipal cemetery could not itself afford, she said, to mount guard across its territory of several wooded hectares (acres), lying on the edge of town in the shadow of dilapidated industrial buildings beside the railway tracks.

"It's awful. They just steal and steal. And what can we do about it?" shrugged Valentina Guseyeva, a pensioner painting and laying plastic flowers at the grave of her sister. But she warned with typical Russian philosophy: "God will punish them."
